In [[mathematics]], a '''right group'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Nagy, Attila|title=Special classes of semigroups|date=2001|publisher=Kluwer Academic Publishers|isbn=0-7923-6890-8|location=Dordrecht|oclc=46240335}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Clifford, A. H.|title=The algebraic theory of semigroups|others=Preston, G. B.|date=29 June 2014|isbn=978-1-4704-1234-0|edition=Reprinted with corrections|location=Providence, Rhode Island|oclc=882503487}}</ref> is an [[algebraic structure]] consisting of a [[set (mathematics)|set]] together with a [[binary operation]] that combines two elements into a third element while obeying the right group [[axiom]]s. The right group axioms are similar to the [[Group (mathematics)|group]] axioms, but while groups can have only one identity and any element can have only one inverse, right groups allow for multiple {{nowrap|one-sided}} [[identity element]]s and multiple  {{nowrap|one-sided}} [[inverse element]]s.

It can be proven (theorem 1.27 in <ref name=":1" />) that a right group is [[isomorphic]] to the [[direct product]] of a [[right zero semigroup]] and a [[Group (mathematics)|group]], while a '''right abelian group'''<ref name=":0" /> is the direct product of a right zero semigroup and an [[abelian group]]. '''Left group'''<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> and '''left abelian group'''<ref name=":0" /> are defined in analogous way, by substituting right for left in the definitions. The rest of this article will be mostly concerned about right groups, but everything applies to left groups by doing the appropriate right/left substitutions.

== Definition ==
A '''right group''', originally called '''multiple group''',<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hollings|first=Christopher D.|date=2017-09-01|title='Nobody could possibly misunderstand what a group is': a study in early twentieth-century group axiomatics|url= |journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences|language=en|volume=71|issue=5|pages=409–481|doi=10.1007/s00407-017-0193-8|issn=1432-0657|pmc=5573778|pmid=28912607}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Clifford|first=A. H.|date=1933|title=A System Arising from a Weakened Set of Group Postulates|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1968703|journal=Annals of Mathematics|volume=34|issue=4|pages=865–871|doi=10.2307/1968703|jstor=1968703|issn=0003-486X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> is a set <math>R</math> with a [[binary operation]] ⋅, satisfying the following axioms:<ref name=":2" />

; Closure
: For all <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> in <math>R</math>, there is an element ''c'' in <math>R</math> such that <math>c = a \cdot b</math>.
; Associativity
: For all <math>a, b, c</math> in <math>R</math>, <math>(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)</math>.
; Left identity element
: There is at least one left identity in <math>R</math>. That is, there exists an element <math>e</math> such that <math>e \cdot a = a</math> for all <math>a</math> in <math>R</math>. Such an element does not need to be unique.
; Right inverse elements
: For every <math>a</math> in <math>R</math> and every identity element <math>e</math>, also in <math>R</math>, there is at least one element <math>b</math> in <math>R</math>, such that <math>a \cdot b = e</math>. Such element <math>b</math> is said to be the [[inverse element|right inverse]] of <math>a</math> with respect to <math>e</math>.

== Examples ==

=== Direct product of finite sets ===
Clifford provides the following example.<ref name=":1" /> Take the group <math>G = \{ e, a, b \}</math>, the right zero semigroup <math>Z = \{ 1, 2 \}</math> and construct a right group <math>R_{gz}</math> as the direct product of <math>G</math> and <math>Z</math>.

<math>G</math> is simply the [[cyclic group]] of [[order (group theory)|order]] 3, with <math>e</math> as its identity, and <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> as the inverses of each other.

|+<math>G</math> table

!''b''
|-

|''b''
|-
!''a''

|''e''
|-
!''b''
|''b''
|''e''
|''a''
|}
<math>Z</math> is the right zero semigroup of order 2. Notice the each element repeats along its column, since by definition <math>x \cdot y = y</math>, for any <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> in <math>Z</math>.
: {| class="wikitable"
|+<math>Z</math> table
!
!1
!2
|-
!1
|1
|2
|-
!2
|1
|2
|}

The [[direct product]] <math>R_{gz} = G \times Z</math> of these two structures is defined as follows:
* The elements of <math>R_{gz}</math> are ordered pairs <math>(g, z)</math> such that <math>g</math> is in <math>G</math> and <math>z</math> is in <math>Z</math>.
* The <math>R_{gz}</math> operation is defined element-wise:
*: Formula 1: <math>(x, y) \cdot (u, v) = (xu, v)</math>

The elements of <math>R_{gz}</math> will look like <math>(e, 1), (e, 2), (a, 1)</math> and so on. For brevity, let's rename these as <math>e_1, e_2, a_1</math>, and so on. The [[Cayley table]] of <math>R_{gz}</math> is as follows:

Here are some facts about <math>R_{gz}</math>:
* <math>R_{gz}</math> has two left identities: <math>e_1</math> and <math>e_2</math>. Some examples:
*: <math>e2 \cdot b1 = b1</math>
*: <math>e1 \cdot a2 = a2</math>
* Each element has two right inverses. For example, the right inverses of <math>a_2</math> with regards to <math>e_1</math> and <math>e_2</math> are <math>b_1</math> and <math>b_2</math>, respectively.
*: <math>a2 \cdot b1 = e1</math>
*: <math>a2 \cdot b2 = e2</math>

=== Complex numbers in polar coordinates ===
Clifford gives a second example<ref name=":2" /> involving [[complex numbers]]. Given two non-zero complex numbers ''a'' and ''b'', the following operation forms a right group:
: <math>a \cdot b = |a|\, b</math>
All complex numbers with [[absolute value|modulus]] equal to 1 are left identities, and all complex numbers will have a right inverse with respect to any left identity.

The inner structure of this right group becomes clear when we use [[Complex number#Polar complex plane|polar coordinates]]: let <math>a = A e^{i \alpha}</math> and <math>b = B e^{i \beta}</math>, where ''A'' and ''B'' are the magnitudes and <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are the [[Complex_number#Polar_complex_plane|arguments]] (angles) of ''a'' and ''b'', respectively. <math>a \cdot b</math> (this is not the regular multiplication of complex numbers) then becomes <math>A e^{i \alpha} \cdot B e^{i \beta} = AB e^{i \beta}</math>. If we represent the magnitudes and arguments as ordered pairs, we can write this as:
: Formula 2: <math>(A, \alpha) \cdot (B,\beta) = (AB, \beta)</math>
This right group is the direct product of a group (positive [[real number]]s under multiplication) and a right zero semigroup induced by the real numbers. Structurally, this is identical to formula 1 above. In fact, this is how all right group operations look like when written as ordered pairs of the direct product of their factors.

=== Complex numbers in cartesian coordinates ===
If we take the and complex numbers and define an operation similar to example 2 but use  cartesian instead of polar coordinates and addition instead of multiplication, we get another right group, with operation defined as follows:
: <math>(a + bi) \cdot (c + di) = a + c + di</math>, or equivalently:
: Formula 3: <math>(a,b) \cdot (c,d) = (a+c,d)</math>

=== A practical example from computer science ===
Consider the following example from computer science, where a set would be implemented as a programming language [[Type system|type]].
* Let <math>X</math> be the set of date times in an arbitrary programming language.
* Let <math>D</math> be the set of transformations equivalent to adding a duration to an element of <math>X</math>. 
* Let <math>Z</math> be the set of time zone transformations on elements of <math>X</math>.

Both <math>D</math> and <math>Z</math> are subsets of <math>T_x</math>, the [[full transformation semigroup]] on <math>X</math>. <math>D</math> behaves like a [[Group (mathematics)|group]], where there is a zero duration and every duration has an inverse duration. If we treat these transformations as [[Semigroup action|right semigroup actions]], <math>Z</math> behaves like a [[right zero semigroup]], such that a time zone transformation always cancels any previous time zone transformation on a given date time.

Given any two arbitrary date times <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> (ignore issues regarding representation boundaries), one can find a pair of a duration and a time zone that will transform <math>a</math> into <math>b</math>. This composite transformation of time zone conversion and duration adding is isomorphic to the right group <math>D \times Z</math>.

Taking the java.time package as an example,<ref>{{Cite web|title=java.time (Java Platform SE 8 )|url=https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/time/package-summary.html|access-date=2021-06-03|website=docs.oracle.com}}</ref> the sets <math>X, D</math> and <math>Z</math> would correspond to the class '''ZonedDateTime''', the function '''plus''' and the function '''withZoneSameInstant''', respectively. More concretely, for any ZonedDateTime ''t''1 and ''t''2, there is a Duration ''d'' and a ZoneId ''z'', such that:
: t2 = t1.plus(d).withZoneSomeInstant(z)

The expression above can be written more concisely using [[Group action#Right group action|right action]] notation borrowed from [[group theory]] as:
: <math>t2 = t1.d.z</math>
It can also be verified that durations and time zones, when viewed as transformations on date/times, in addition to obeying the axioms of groups and right zero semigroups, respectively, they commute with each other. That is, for any date/time t, any duration d and any timezone z:
: <math>t.d.z = t.z.d</math>
This is the same as saying:
: <math>d \cdot z = z \cdot d</math>
